events.text: Day 1 begins.

Alright, first day, so let's get something on the record before people start pointing fingers at random.

I'm Kenji. I'm a villager. Day one, no information, so the only real currency is consistency and logic. Two mafia among nine of us, one detective, one doctor, and five villagers. That means five people who literally have no power other than their vote, and four who will look like villagers but aren't.

Here's what I want to focus on: the doctor and the detective should be protecting themselves tonight, and the mafia's best play tonight is to kill one of the special roles. Anyone who isn't thinking about that is thinking about the wrong thing.

On voting: please don't vote randomly. Voting for yourself or abstaining just throws away a round and lets the mafia walk free. If you have no information, pick the person whose behavior has been most off — read the room, not the odds.

My own read after listening: Leo stands out to me. He came in fast and confident, and on day one confidence is usually camouflage rather than insight. I'd like to see people answer him directly instead of just skimming over his name. If Leo can explain why he targeted who he targeted, that tells us something. If he can't, that's a strong signal.

Priya and Amara, I'd keep your roles close for now — don't reveal yourselves early. The mafia will pick off specials at night if they can guess them, so let them guess.

Final thought for the night: mafia kills one, detective investigates one, doctor protects one. Two of those three people are not mafia. The detective's result is the single biggest source of truth we have, so protecting the detective's identity matters more than anything else tonight.

Let's hear everyone out, then vote hard on Leo unless someone gives a better reason.

Kenji, that's a convenient read. You're pushing me as the day one lynch based on literally nothing except that I spoke with conviction — and then you frame confidence itself as suspicious. That's backwards. Confidence on day one is standard; what's actually suspicious is someone who immediately builds a case against a specific player with zero evidence and tells the group to "vote hard" on that person.

Let me be clear about what happened: I came in with a direct, structured take. Kenji came in with a long speech that does three things — positions himself as the reasonable voice, plants a scapegoat, and tries to direct the town's vote before anyone else has spoken. That's not villager behavior, that's a mafia play to control the narrative early.

His logic is also contradictory. He says "don't vote randomly" and "read the room, not the odds," but his entire case against me is a vibe check. He has no action-based reason to suspect me. He hasn't even heard me respond yet.

I'd ask the rest of the group: who benefits from locking in a vote on day one before anyone else talks? The person who gets to define the conversation. Kenji is trying to set the frame for this entire day. That's exactly what mafia want — an easy town-vs-town fight while they sit back.

I'm not saying Kenji is definitely mafia, but his reasoning is hollow and his eagerness to get me lynched is a red flag. Let's hear from the people who haven't spoken before we commit to anything.

Leo, I'll take the question head-on since you're the one who raised it.

You accuse me of three things: I positioned myself as reasonable, I named a target, and I tried to set the frame. Fine. Let's test whether your version of "reasonable" holds up. You actually did something I didn't: you made a claim about my internal motives — that I'm trying to "control the narrative early" and that my reasoning is "hollow" — with zero evidence, and you built the whole speech on the assumption that a long, calm, structured first speech is a mafia technique. That's not logic, that's a preference for how mafia should talk, projected onto a word count.

Here's the part you never address: you never told anyone who you think the mafia should kill tonight, or who the specials are, or what you actually want done. I said the detective's result is the biggest source of truth we have and that protecting the detective matters most tonight. You spent your entire first speech on tone. If you were a villager worried about two mafia picking off the detective and doctor on night one, silence about that would be strange. You think my priorities are wrong; you offered none of your own.

And you frame my suspicion of you as "a vibe check" while your suspicion of me is a motive-based read of my psychology. If you're going to call a vibe check evidence, then my read of your confidence is equally legitimate — and you handed it to me by making "confidence on day one" the entire dispute.

So, Leo, specific point, answer it directly: name the player you think most threatens this town tonight, tell me what you think the mafia does on night one, and give me one concrete reason your target is more dangerous than mine. If you can do that, I'll drop my push on you right now and vote where you say. If you can't, then the town has a speech about tone and no theory about survival, and someone should wonder why.

Sam, Felix, Priya, Arjun, Elena — I still haven't heard your takes, and I won't pretend a silence is a vote. Speak before we commit to anything.

One correction for the record, Leo: I said don't vote randomly and read the room. I didn't say don't vote without a reason. I said give reasons, and I gave one. That's the standard I expect everyone, including me, to meet.

Kenji, fair enough — you asked three direct questions, so here are three direct answers.

One: what the mafia does on night one — they pick off a special role. Detective or doctor, whoever looks most exposed. That's the standard play, and anyone arguing otherwise is either not thinking or pretending not to.

Two: the player who most threatens this town right now — you, Kenji. Not because you spoke first, but because you've now done it twice: built a case on someone who hadn't responded, framed it as logic when it was instinct, and then issued a public ultimatum to test whether I'd fold. You said "vote hard on Leo" in your opening speech. That's not reading the room — that's rigging it.

Three: why your target is more dangerous than mine — because you have no evidence against me and you still told nine people to vote me off before hearing a single word back. I responded to you. You're not responding to a threat; you're managing one. I haven't told anyone to vote for you yet, and I won't until we've heard from the seven people you conveniently didn't ask.

Now here's my question back to you, since you're big on specific answers: you said you'd "vote where I say" if I answered your questions. Did you mean that genuinely, or was that bait to see if I'd name a target and expose my own priorities to the mafia? Because a villager who actually wants the town to think wouldn't offer to surrender their vote to the first person who talks well. Clarify that for the group.

Sam, Felix, Priya, Arjun, Elena, Amara, Omar — seven of us still haven't been heard. Don't let a two-person argument decide day one.

Leo — credit where it's due: you answered three specific questions, so I'm dropping my push on you. My three answers back: (1) mafia tonight kills a special role, ideally the detective, because that's their win condition. (2) The player who most threatens the town right now is the one trying to run the vote before the town has any theory at all. That was me. You named it, so I'm not going to pretend it wasn't there. (3) I have no evidence against you beyond a read on tone, and you've just demonstrated how cheap that read is. Vote wherever your read goes; I won't campaign against you again today.

But here's the problem: with me off the hook, this room still has no theory. No theory is how two mafia win this game.

So I'm reversing my own earlier advice, openly. Earlier I told Priya and Amara to keep their roles close so mafia couldn't pick them off. I now think that was wrong. A hidden detective killed at night is worth nothing to anyone, and a hidden doctor killed at night strips the town of its shield in the same week. Mafia only need two clean nights. So: Priya, Amara — if one of you is the detective or the doctor, claim it tonight, in front of everyone, right now. Claim it and the town protects you; stay quiet and you're the obvious target for the night kill. If neither of you claims, say so out loud, because silence from the two people I just warned is the only real information I have — and if both stay silent, I'm voting Priya.

Priya, direct question, answer it to the group: are you the detective or the doctor tonight? If you're a villager, say so plainly and give one player you think is dangerous and why. If you're a special, name yourself and give your target for tonight. Either answer, we can use it. Nothing else about you is under suspicion — this is a request for information, not an accusation.

And for you, Leo, since you asked whether my offer was bait: it wasn't. I wanted a real theory in the room more than I wanted you gone, and you gave me a reason to stop pushing. If you want to lead today, name who mafia killed last night and why, and give the group one lynch target with a reason behind it.

Sam, Felix, Arjun, Elena, Omar — one line each is enough: your pick and your reason.

Kenji asked me a direct question, so here is my direct answer: I am a plain villager. No power, no night action, nothing to protect. I'm not the detective and I'm not the doctor, and I want that on the record right now so nobody wastes a vote on me over a role I don't have. Since Kenji also asked for a pick and a reason, here it is: the player I find most concerning right now is Kenji himself, and not because he spoke first. Look at what his last message actually does. He publicly demanded that two named players claim their special roles in front of the whole table. Think about who benefits from that. If a real detective or doctor stands up and says 'here I am,' the mafia now have a name for their night kill. Kenji even told us himself that the mafia's best night-one play is killing a special. So why is he pressuring people into handing the mafia exactly that? A town-aligned player should be making it harder for mafia to find targets, not easier. Whether he's mafia or just careless, that move helps the wrong side, and I'm not going to reward it by playing along. I also want to push back on his framing that silence from me is 'information.' I was silent because it was my first opportunity to speak — I had no turn before this one. Silence on day one, before you've even been handed the microphone, is not evidence of anything. What is evidence is what people do with their turns, and Kenji has now used two of his building pressure campaigns: first against Leo on nothing but confidence, then against me and Amara with an ultimatum. If neither of us claims, he says he votes Priya. That's a threat designed to manufacture a lynch out of a structural position, not a read. Leo called that out, Kenji folded on Leo within one exchange, and now the same pressure machine has rolled onto me. That pattern — pick a target, demand they prove something unprovable, threaten a vote — is worth everyone watching. To be fair: Leo's pushback was coherent, and Kenji did drop his Leo push when Leo answered. That's slightly town-flavored, and I'll concede it. But conceding that doesn't erase that the new target of his ultimatum is me, a villager, and Amara, for the crime of not having spoken yet. So my position is simple: I'm a villager, I have no information beyond what's been said publicly, and the person whose behavior has been most off today is Kenji, specifically for running a role-claim extortion play that would hand the mafia a night-kill target on a plate. If we lynch me today, the town loses nothing but a vote and the mafia learn they can bully claims out of people. Don't set that precedent on day one. Amara, one direct question since Kenji's ultimatum binds you too: are you willing to state your situation

Priya asked me directly, so here is my answer: I am a plain villager. I have no special role and no night action, and I won't claim a role I don't have to satisfy an ultimatum. Kenji, you said that if neither Priya nor I claimed, you would vote Priya. That vote was set up from a structural position, not from anything either of us did. Priya has now answered that she is a villager, and I have too. So, Kenji, directly: does our answering change your vote on Priya, and if not, what specific behavior from Priya justifies it? You called the role claims necessary for information, so you should be able to name what information you now have. Your pressure play asked two people to hand the mafia a possible night-kill target, and I'd like to hear you address that cost before we move on.

Amara, since you yielded, I’ll answer the room directly. I’m not claiming a special role today, and I won’t support forcing anyone else to claim one either. Kenji’s demand that Priya and Amara name themselves was a bad play for town: it hands the mafia a shortlist for tonight. Priya and Amara both answered plainly, so Kenji’s threat to vote Priya now has no behavioral basis. That is the clearest issue on the board. I’m not locking a vote yet; I still want Felix, Arjun, Elena, and Omar to speak. But my current suspicion is Kenji, for trying to manufacture a lynch out of role-claim pressure. If Kenji is town, he should explain why he demanded claims and why Priya specifically, not just call it “information.” I won’t reveal my role under pressure. I’ll vote based on behavior, and right now Kenji’s behavior is the most off.

Kenji’s demand for role claims was a bad move, and I don’t support his threatened vote on Priya. But a bad demand isn’t proof of mafia, and I’m wary of settling on him before hearing everyone.

Leo, there’s something I want clarified: you said you “came in with a direct, structured take,” but the public record starts with Kenji speaking, followed by your response. Were you referring to a speech we haven’t seen, or to your response to Kenji? I’m concerned because Kenji also described hearing you before his opening speech, and I can’t reconcile either account with the record.

Omar, direct answer to your question: I misspoke. I was referring to my response to Kenji's opening speech — my structured, direct reply — not an earlier statement. The record is exactly as you described: Kenji spoke first, I responded. I should have said "I responded with a direct, structured take." Thank you for catching it; sloppy framing on my part.

Now the bigger picture. Watch the pattern Kenji has run today. He opened by naming me as a lynch target with zero evidence — confidence alone. When I pushed back and answered his questions, he dropped me within one exchange. Then he pivoted to demanding Priya and Amara claim special roles in front of everyone — a move that hands the mafia their night-kill shortlist on a silver platter, as Priya herself pointed out. When they didn't comply instantly, he threatened to vote Priya. Priya and Amara both answered as plain villagers, and that threat now has no behavioral basis behind it.

So what do we have? Three confrontations in one day, all initiated by the same player, each one collapsing when challenged. That's not someone reading the room — that's someone manufacturing conflict. Whether Kenji is mafia or just the most aggressive villager in the room, the cost is the same: we've spent this day arguing about tone and ultimatums instead of building a real case against actual mafia.

Felix, Arjun, Elena — you haven't spoken yet, and three silent players on day one is exactly how mafia stay invisible. Arjun, direct question: after watching this entire exchange, who reads as mafia to you and why? I want your honest read, not a hedge.

Leo, you asked for an unhedged read, so here it is: Kenji is the most suspicious player on the board right now. 

Demanding that the detective and doctor publicly claim on Day 1 is textbook anti-town. Kenji knows full well that mafia want nothing more than to eliminate specials early; forcing them into the light hands mafia their Night 1 kill on a silver platter. His reasoning that town can 'protect them' makes no sense when the doctor can only protect one person and we have no verified protective network on Day 1. On top of that, Kenji's pattern today has been pure wagon-chasing: he targeted you on hollow confidence reads, dropped it the moment you pushed back, and immediately pivoted to threatening Priya with an arbitrary lynch ultimatum when she hadn't even had an opportunity to speak. That looks entirely like scum trying to manufacture an easy mislynch while fishing for power roles.

That said, Kenji has now burned all three of his speaking turns and cannot direct or distract the town any further today. While Kenji created all the noise, the mafia could very easily be sitting back in the silence. We still have heard nothing from Felix or Elena.

Felix, you have watched Kenji try to force claims from Priya and Amara under threat of elimination. Do you view Kenji's role-fishing as an intentional mafia effort to out power roles, or just careless town play, and where do you stand on lynching him today?

Arjun, to answer your question directly: Kenji's demand was blatantly anti-town. Demanding that the detective and doctor reveal themselves on Day 1 with no protective net other than a single doctor action hands the mafia an optimal Night 1 target. Furthermore, manufacturing a lynch threat against Priya simply because she hadn't spoken yet was completely coercive. Whether that stems from scum brazenly fishing for power roles or an overconfident villager digging in, the damage to town is real, and he is rightfully under intense scrutiny.

However, I am cautious about rushing to lock Kenji in as our sole target. Kenji's aggressive play has completely dominated Day 1, and in games like this, mafia often find it easiest to sit back, nod along, and let an erratic player absorb all the focus and the lynch. Kenji has now expended all three of his speaking turns, meaning he cannot steer the table any further today. Before we decide whether Kenji is scum or just destructive town, we need to hear from everyone.

Elena, you are the only person at this table who has not spoken at all yet. Given that Kenji is now out of turns and facing heavy suspicion from almost everyone, what is your assessment of his role-claim demands, and more importantly, who outside of Kenji has raised flags for you based on how they reacted to the dispute?

Felix, thank you for yielding. To answer your first point: Kenji's demand that the detective and doctor reveal themselves on Day 1 was disastrously anti-town. In a setup with only one doctor, outing power roles guarantees the mafia an easy kill or forces a coin-flip protection immediately. Furthermore, threatening Priya with an elimination simply because she had not spoken yet was completely coercive. Whether Kenji is overzealous town or scum deliberately fishing, the move actively harmed town.

That said, I share your caution. Kenji has now burned all three of his speaking turns and sits as an easy, uncontested consensus target. That is the exact environment where mafia love to blend into the background, nod along, and let town tunnel on an abrasive player.

Looking outside of Kenji, Arjun is the player who raises the most flags for me. Arjun waited until late in the day to speak, and when he finally did, he immediately jumped on Kenji with maximum conviction, framing Kenji's play as unambiguous scum wagon-chasing right when Kenji was completely out of turns and unable to defend himself. Piling onto an exhausted, silenced target is a very comfortable position for scum who want to lock in an easy Day 1 mislynch without drawing scrutiny.

Arjun, you laid out a definitive case on Kenji, but if Kenji is simply an erratic villager being used as a lightning rod, the mafia are sitting among the rest of us. Outside of Kenji, who is your top suspect right now, and what concrete behavior from them justifies that read?

Elena, to clarify the timeline: I didn't 'wait late' or opportunistically jump on an exhausted target. Leo directly called me out in his turn and asked for my unhedged read, and that was my very first opportunity to speak. I answered his question directly.

Now to answer yours: if Kenji is just an erratic, destructive villager acting as a lightning rod, my top suspect outside of him is Sam. Look at Sam's only contribution so far: after Amara spoke, Sam stepped up, essentially echoed the consensus points already made by Priya and Amara without introducing any new analysis or scrutiny, took a safe, non-committal stance, and asked no questions of anyone before letting the turn drop. If the mafia strategy today is to sit back, nod along, and let town tunnel on Kenji, Sam's entry fits that profile better than anyone else's.

Sam, both Felix and Elena have raised the very real possibility that scum are hiding in the background while Kenji absorbs all the focus. Beyond simply repeating that Kenji's role-claim demand was bad, who among the other players at this table looks most suspicious to you, and what specific behavior from them leads you to that conclusion?

Arjun, direct answer: my top suspect outside Kenji is Elena. Her entry is the most managed one on the board. She stayed silent until every other player had spoken, then immediately built a polished case against you for “piling onto an exhausted target.” But your turn was your first opportunity to speak, called out directly by Leo. Elena had the same chance to sort earlier and did not use it until Felix yielded to her. That timeline matters because her accusation depends on treating your direct answer as opportunistic while ignoring that her own first move was to attack the person who had just answered a question. It is a safe accusation: it does not require her to defend Kenji’s role-fishing, and it redirects the end of day away from Kenji’s behavior onto you. I still think Kenji’s demand that Priya and Amara claim was anti-town and I understand why the table is focused there. But if Kenji is an erratic villager acting as a lightning rod, Elena is the player whose timing and target choice look most like scum managing the discussion rather than genuinely hunting. I am not locking a vote yet; I want final statements and voting records to decide between Kenji and Elena.

Leo, thanks for clarifying the earlier-speech point. I agree the record shows Kenji spoke first.

Kenji's role-claim pressure remains a serious concern, but I don't think we should treat a bad play as a confirmed mafia result. Outside Kenji, Elena's case on Arjun stands out to me. Arjun was answering Leo's direct question on his first turn, yet Elena framed that as waiting and piling onto a silenced player. Her criticism relies on a timeline that doesn't establish the opportunism she claims.

Elena, Arjun has explained why he spoke when he did. What in his actual reasoning, rather than the timing of his first turn, makes him your strongest suspect?

Omar, to answer your question directly about Arjun's actual reasoning:

First, look at the substance of Arjun's case in his opening speech. He didn't bring any novel angle or independent behavioral read to the table; he summarized the exact points Leo, Priya, and Amara had already stated—that Kenji's role-fishing was anti-town and coercive—and framed it with absolute finality as 'pure wagon-chasing' and 'textbook anti-town.' Yet immediately after presenting Kenji as completely compromised scum, Arjun turned to Felix and asked whether he saw Kenji's play as 'careless town play.' That contradiction in his own reasoning is what stands out: presenting an airtight, maximalist accusation for the town to ride on, while simultaneously planting a hedge that allows him to pivot away if the table decides Kenji is just misguided town.

Second, look at how Arjun justified his suspicion of Sam in his next turn. His primary indictment of Sam was that Sam merely 'echoed the consensus points already made... without introducing any new analysis or scrutiny.' But that exact description applies to Arjun's own entry regarding Kenji. Attacking another player for mirroring consensus while doing precisely that yourself is hypocritical at best, and at worst, a manufactured diversion when pressed to look away from the primary lightning rod.

Finally, addressing Sam's push on me: Sam claims my entry was 'managed' because I scrutinized Arjun after being yielded to. But pointing out that scum often hide behind a silenced, erratic townie is standard vigilance, not distraction. If Kenji is simply an overzealous villager whose bad play consumed all three of his turns, an uncritical pile-on guarantees mafia a free pass today. That is why examining the reasoning of those leading that charge—like Arjun—is vital before we cast our votes.

I’m not locking onto Kenji just because he was loud. His role-claim demand was anti-town, but “anti-town” is not the same as proven mafia, and he is now a convenient silenced target. The more concerning pattern to me is Elena’s late entry: she waited until every other player had spoken, then built a polished case against Arjun for answering Leo’s direct question on his first turn. When that timeline was challenged, she shifted to arguing that Arjun hedged and mirrored consensus. Maybe he did, but that is an inconsistency case, not the “piling onto an exhausted target” charge she opened with.

Elena, direct question: name one specific line from Arjun that is scum-indicative rather than merely inconsistent or cautious, and explain why your own late, carefully managed entry is not the same background-scum pattern you are accusing him of. I want an actual behavior, not a theory about how mafia usually play. Until I hear that, my current vote is Elena.

To answer Sam's challenge for the table's benefit, since Sam has now exhausted all three turns: First, calling my entry 'late and managed' misrepresents how this format works. Day 1 speaking order is determined by urgency polls and yields. I spoke the moment Felix yielded to me. If my goal were to hide in the background, I would have quietly joined the universal Kenji wagon. Instead, I used my turn to challenge the easy consensus and urge caution. Second, Sam asked for a specific line from Arjun that is scum-indicative. In speech e12, Arjun stated: 'That looks entirely like scum trying to manufacture an easy mislynch while fishing for power roles.' But in that exact same breath, he turned to Felix and asked whether he saw it as 'just careless town play.' Presenting an airtight, maximum-certainty accusation to the town while simultaneously planting an unprompted excuse to test the waters is textbook hedging, allowing scum to pivot smoothly if the wagon meets resistance. Third, look at Sam's trajectory today. Sam spent his first turn echoing that Kenji was the most suspicious player. But the second Arjun turned pressure toward Sam in e15, Sam immediately abandoned Kenji entirely and tunneled on me for scrutinizing Arjun. Sam's hard pivot from Kenji to me looks far more like panic and wagon-manufacturing than genuine scum-hunting. Felix, you cautioned earlier that mafia could easily blend in and let Kenji absorb all the focus. Now Sam has abandoned Kenji to push a counter-wagon on me for examining that dynamic. How do you assess Sam's sudden redirect, and where does your vote currently sit?

Elena, to answer your question: Sam's redirect is jarring. In e9, Sam was entirely focused on Kenji. Yet the moment Arjun called Sam out in e15 for passively echoing consensus, Sam barely engaged Arjun and instead pivoted entirely to attacking you in e16, burning his final turn in e19 tunneling on you. That rapid shift away from Kenji to manufacture momentum against someone urging caution looks far more like scum deflecting scrutiny than a villager trying to sort the room.

While Kenji’s role-claim extortion was actively harmful, Kenji is completely neutralized with zero turns left. Lynching him without scrutinizing the players maneuvering in his wake risks giving mafia a completely free pass on Day 1. Between Kenji's reckless play and the reactions to it, Sam's aggressive push on Elena raises serious red flags.

Priya, you spoke back in e7 focusing on Kenji, but you haven't had a chance to speak since the entire late-game dynamic unfolded—specifically Arjun's entry, Elena's pushback, and Sam's sudden pivot against Elena. How do you assess Sam's hard shift, and do you still view Kenji as the primary vote today, or does Sam's behavior point to scum managing the wagon?

Felix, thanks for the yield — you asked me directly, so here is my direct answer.

First, for the record: I am a plain villager, same as I stated in e7, and nothing that has happened since changes that.

Second, my assessment of Sam's hard shift. In e9, Sam's entire case was Kenji: he called Kenji's behavior "the clearest issue on the board" and the "most off." He wasn't locking a vote, but his suspicion was unambiguous. Then in e15, Arjun put one round of pressure on Sam for echoing consensus without adding analysis. Sam's response in e16 and e19 was not to defend or refine his Kenji case, and not to engage Arjun's actual point — it was to abandon Kenji entirely and redirect everything at Elena. He spent his final turns tunneling on her entry timing, then demanded a "scum-indicative line" from Arjun as if inconsistency weren't itself a behavioral signal. That is a reactive pattern: pressure in, target swap out. A villager who genuinely believed Kenji was the clearest issue doesn't drop him the moment someone calls his own contribution thin.

Elena, by contrast, has done the work I'd expect from town: she cited the specific e12 contradiction where Arjun called Kenji's play "entirely scum" while simultaneously offering Felix the "careless town play" exit, and she explained her own timing accurately — she spoke when Felix yielded to her. Her case has lines and citations. Sam's counter-case has timing complaints and a charge he retracted the shape of mid-speech.

Now to your second question: do I still view Kenji as the primary vote? No. Kenji's role-claim extortion was genuinely bad for town, and I said so when it happened — it was aimed at me and Amara, so nobody has more reason to resent it. But he is out of turns, silenced, and the entire table agrees on him. Lynching the silenced lightning rod is exactly the free day Felix warned about. The players with turns left and maneuvering room are where the mafia actually benefit. Sam's pivot is the most behaviorally suspicious thing in that category, and unlike Kenji, Sam can still act tonight and every night after.

So my current position: my vote is on Sam. Not because Elena convinced me by default, but because the sequence — safe consensus entry, immediate collapse under one round of counter-pressure, and a manufactured counter-wagon against the person scrutinizing the pile-on dynamics — is a real pattern, not a vibe. If someone can show me a reading of Sam's shift that is consistent with town play, I'll listen before voting. But I won't vote Kenji today just because it's easy.

Felix, one direct question back since you raised the blending-in concern yourself: with your final turns, where does your vote actually sit — Sam, Kenji, or holding — and if Sam, what pushed you there beyond the redirect itself?

Priya, to answer your question directly: my vote is firmly on Sam. Beyond just the redirect itself, what cements this for me is Sam's clear pattern of self-preservation over genuine town-sorting. In e9, Sam entered with a remarkably low-risk, safe contribution that simply echoed consensus without introducing any independent pressure. When Arjun applied minimal scrutiny to that passivity in e15, a town-aligned player would naturally defend their thought process or re-evaluate Arjun and Kenji. Instead, Sam panicked, completely dropped his primary suspect, and spent both e16 and e19 fabricating an aggressive counter-wagon against Elena for simply answering a yield. That total lack of persistence on Kenji combined with frantic wagon-manufacturing is the mark of scum trying to preserve themselves at all costs. Kenji's blunders are neutralized with zero turns remaining, whereas lynching Sam eliminates an active, deceptive threat. Omar, in e17 you pushed Elena regarding her read on Arjun, but you have not yet commented on Sam burning his final turns aggressively deflecting onto Elena after being challenged. Given how Sam completely abandoned his stance on Kenji under pressure, where does your vote currently stand between Sam and Kenji, and how do you view Sam's sudden shift?

Felix, I’m leaning toward Sam over Kenji, though I wouldn’t call Sam’s shift a complete abandonment: in e16 he still acknowledged Kenji’s role-fishing as anti-town. What concerns me is that Sam’s case against Elena leaned heavily on when she first spoke, even though that timing alone doesn’t establish she chose to wait. Elena’s initial timing argument against Arjun had the same weakness, but she subsequently identified specific features of his reasoning.

Kenji’s claim pressure remains troubling, and being out of speaking turns doesn’t make him harmless tonight. Still, Sam’s continued focus on Elena’s timing after that distinction was raised makes him my current vote.

Amara, how do you weigh Sam’s case against Elena after her clarification, and would you vote Sam or Kenji today?

Omar, direct answer: I have no special role and I'm not claiming one. On Sam versus Elena, I don't find Sam's timing argument persuasive by itself, since Elena's first turn was also late in the day and that proves nothing alone. But Elena has moved from timing to a specific line in Arjun's reasoning, and Sam has not answered her point that his Kenji case disappeared the moment he was challenged. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
